query.explanation: `pluck` pushes the column list into the SELECT clause and returns raw values, so SQLite only sends the id column over the wire. `Post.all.map(&:id)` would instead issue `SELECT "posts".*` and build one model object per row, which is why pluck is the cheaper choice for id lists.

questions.rationale: pluck builds a narrow `SELECT "posts"."id"`; it never instantiates models, so no other column and no `*` appears in the statement.

class Post < ActiveRecord::Base
  has_many :comments
end
class Comment < ActiveRecord::Base
  belongs_to :post, counter_cache: true
end

post = Post.find(id) # posts.comments_count exists

query.explanation: On an unloaded has_many, `size` normally issues `SELECT COUNT(*)`. When the inverse `belongs_to` declares `counter_cache: true` and the owner carries a `comments_count` column, `size` returns that cached integer with no SQL at all. `count` would still hit the database, which is the usual trap.
query.title: counter caches make size free

questions.rationale: with a counter cache column present, `size` reads the already loaded `comments_count` attribute instead of sending a COUNT, so zero queries run.

questions.prompt: does reading title here raise activemodel missingattributeerror?
questions.code:
post = Post.select(:id).first
post.title

query.explanation: `select(:id)` is a real optimisation: only the id travels from the database. The cost is that the model is partial, so any attribute reader outside the selected list raises `ActiveModel::MissingAttributeError`. Always select every column the surrounding code will touch, or load the full row.
query.title: partial selects and missing attributes

questions.rationale: narrowing the SELECT list leaves title entirely absent from the attribute set, and ActiveRecord raises rather than silently returning nil.

Post.where(id: id).update_all(views: 5)
after  = Post.find(id).updated_at

query.explanation: `update_all` is fast because it writes a single UPDATE for the whole relation without instantiating records. That speed comes from skipping validations, callbacks and automatic timestamps, so `updated_at` is untouched. Add `updated_at: Time.current` to the hash yourself when consumers rely on it.
query.title: update_all skips the model layer

questions.rationale: `update_all` compiles one raw UPDATE statement and bypasses the model layer, so timestamp bumping and callbacks never run and updated_at keeps its old value.

questions.code: Author.joins(:posts).first.posts.loaded?

query.explanation: `joins` builds an INNER JOIN for filtering or ordering but discards the joined columns, so `author.posts` remains unloaded and triggers an N+1 on access. Use `includes`, `preload` or `eager_load` when you actually need the associated records in memory.
query.title: joins does not eager load

questions.rationale: `joins` only adds an INNER JOIN so rows can be filtered; it never populates the association target, so the collection is still unloaded and would query on first access.

questions.prompt: Which join construct appears in the SQL for this relation?

questions.code: Author.eager_load(:posts).to_sql

query.explanation: `eager_load` forces the single-query strategy: it emits a LEFT OUTER JOIN with aliased columns for both tables so authors without posts still appear in the result, then splits the flat rows into objects. An INNER JOIN would silently drop childless authors, which is why `joins` and `eager_load` are not interchangeable.
query.title: eager_load builds one outer join

rel.pluck(:id)

query.explanation: `pluck` checks `loaded? && all_attributes_loaded?`: if the relation has materialised complete records, it simply plucks the attribute from those objects, so no round trip happens. Had the relation been narrowed with `select(:title)`, the id would be missing and a fresh query would be required.

questions.rationale: when the relation is already loaded with full records, pluck maps the requested attribute off the in-memory objects instead of issuing a new SELECT.

questions.prompt: is the second count served from the query cache?
questions.code:
ActiveRecord::Base.cache do
  Post.count
  Post.count
end

query.explanation: Within `ActiveRecord::Base.cache` (wrapped around every request by default in Rails), repeated identical SELECTs are answered from an in-memory hash keyed by SQL and bind values. The notification for the second call carries `cached: true`. Any write, or leaving the block, clears the cache.
query.title: the ActiveRecord query cache

questions.rationale: inside a cache block ActiveRecord memoises results by sql plus binds, so the identical second COUNT is replayed from memory and is reported as a cached query.

questions.prompt: Does the permitted result include the tags key?

params = ActionController::Parameters.new(user: { name: "Ada" })

puts params.to_unsafe_h[:user].is_a?(ActionController::Parameters)
questions.prompt: Is the nested value from to_unsafe_h an ActionController::Parameters?

query.explanation: Both to_h and to_unsafe_h run convert_parameters_to_hashes recursively, returning an ActiveSupport::HashWithIndifferentAccess whose nested hashes and arrays contain hashes, not Parameters. Only params[:user] on the Parameters object gives you Parameters back.
query.title: to_unsafe_h converts deeply

questions.rationale: to_unsafe_h converts the whole structure back to ActiveSupport::HashWithIndifferentAccess, so nested values are plain indifferent hashes rather than Parameters objects.

questions.code:
require 'action_controller'

params = ActionController::Parameters.new(a: 1, b: 2)
permitted = params.permit(:a, :b)

puts permitted.except(:a).permitted?
questions.prompt: Does the result of except still report permitted?

query.explanation: Methods like except, slice, and reject use new_instance_with_inherited_permitted_status, copying the @permitted flag to the new Parameters. That means the derived object can still be passed to to_h or a model without re-permitting.
query.title: except/slice inherit permitted status

questions.rationale: except builds a new instance with inherited permitted status, so slicing keys off an already permitted Parameters keeps the permitted flag instead of resetting it.
